tier_reason: The benchmark code is public (bemayer/xml-benchmark benchmarks/rapidxml/bench.cpp and benchmarks/libxml2/bench.cpp; Debian bookworm g++, CMake Release, -fpermissive), but no CPU model is published (only 'ubuntu-latest / GitHub Actions'), so it is not A. The suite is a 1-star, unlicensed repo created 2026-04-06, not a well-known independent suite, so it is not B either (same call as earlier small third-party harnesses); C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: bemayer/xml-benchmark DOM Parse, run of 2026-09-01 (the page regenerates monthly). RapidXML vs libxml2 throughput: 1084.9 vs 278.8 MB/s in the 10MB bucket (26.93 vs 104.783 ms, ~3.9x, derived from page data); 638.2 vs 161.2 MB/s in the 100MB bucket (163.388 vs 646.685 ms, ~4.0x, derived from page data); 989.0 vs 79.1 MB/s in the 1KB bucket (~12.5x, derived from page data, but at 0.001 vs 0.013 ms, near timer resolution). libxml2 shows higher throughput in the 100KB bucket (3277.1 vs 2017.2 MB/s) and the 1MB bucket (2265.9 vs 1212.7 MB/s). Those buckets include deep files that libxml2 stops parsing partway through (see caveats). pugixml beats RapidXML in every bucket (e.g. 1575.1 vs 1084.9 MB/s at 10MB).
corrections.workload: DOM parse (bemayer/xml-benchmark: 14 libraries across 7 languages, 12 with DOM rows). Each bucket averages a synthetic wide/shallow file and a deep/narrow file. Every library runs in its own debian:bookworm-slim Docker container on a GitHub Actions ubuntu-latest runner, with /usr/bin/time capturing RSS and CPU. The 1KB-100MB size labels are only nominal. Because generate_data.py indents every level, the deep files are about 5.6 MiB (100KB label), 47.9 MiB (1MB and 10MB labels) and 100 MiB (100MB label), with 1,706 to 5,000 nesting levels. Only averages across the two shapes are published.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: g++ from the debian:bookworm-slim image (bookworm's g++ is 12.2.0; the suite never prints the version). The Dockerfile runs cmake -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release (CMake's default GCC Release flags are -O3 -DNDEBUG), and benchmarks/rapidxml/CMakeLists.txt adds CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD 17 and -fpermissive. RapidXml is the SourceForge rapidxml-1.13.zip. libxml2 is Debian's prebuilt package (bookworm: 2.9.14), built with the same Release setup.
corrections.hardware: GitHub Actions ubuntu-latest runner, with each library in a debian:bookworm-slim Docker container (CPU model not published)
corrections.is_fork_of: https://sourceforge.net/projects/rapidxml (not a GitHub fork: externpro/rapidxml imports the upstream RapidXml 1.0-1.13 releases by Marcin Kalicinski and adds CMake/externpro packaging)
corrections.stars_or_usage: 2 stars on externpro/rapidxml, a CMake-packaged mirror. Upstream RapidXml's SourceForge page showed '3,065 This Week' downloads on 2026-09-25. bemayer/xml-benchmark uses the SourceForge rapidxml-1.13.zip as its RapidXML entry. The verifier did not check the SpeedyXml-cpp mention.
corrections.caveats: Only evidence is bemayer/xml-benchmark, a small third-party suite (1 star, no license, created 2026-04-06). It benchmarks the SourceForge rapidxml-1.13.zip, not this repo, though the parser code is the same 1.13. Its size buckets are misleading: deep-shape files are 5.6-100 MiB with up to 5,000 nesting levels. libxml2 2.9.14 (Debian bookworm) stops at depth 256 without XML_PARSE_HUGE (parser.c nodePush calls xmlHaltParser). The libxml2 bench calls xmlParseMemory without checking the result, so its deep-file times measure a halted partial parse. This favors libxml2, so the ~3.9-4.0x RapidXml win at 10MB/100MB is if anything conservative. The 'libxml2 faster at 100KB/1MB' result is probably this artifact. Per-shape numbers are not published. The run is a single monthly run on a CI runner with no CPU model. RapidXml loses to pugixml at every size, so cite only libxml2 as the beaten baseline. RapidXml is a non-validating in-situ parser, while libxml2 builds a full DOM. The upstream parser has had no release since 1.13 (header dated 2009; SourceForge last updated 2013-04-26). externpro's recent commits (last 2026-08-31) are CMake/CI packaging only, so 'active' reflects packaging, not parser development.

notes: The numbers match the page's embedded BENCHMARK_DATA (gh-pages index.html, run 2026-09-01), but the page updates monthly. I downgraded B to C because the suite is not well-known and no CPU model is given. I also found a methodology flaw in the suite: libxml2 stops at its 256-depth limit on the deep files, which biases the results toward libxml2, not RapidXml. I set maintenance_status to active by the last-commit rule, and set is_fork_of to the SourceForge upstream, following the lrstar precedent.

tier_reason: These are first-party README numbers with the CPU stated (i7-4850HQ at a fixed 2.3 GHz). No compiler or flags are stated, and the benchmark harness (tmp/benchmark/orchestrator.sh, the runners, the data generator, tools/rss_sampler.py) is not in the public repo, which has 61 files and no bench or test code. So it is not A, and with no paper or third-party suite it is C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Base-clock run 165913 (15.09.2026, i7-4850HQ at 2.3 GHz, no turbo): 245.7 vs 206.3 MB/s (1 MB), 261.4 vs 227.8 (5 MB) and 285.2 vs 229.2 (10 MB) against pugixml 1.16 in-situ. The README states this as 1.19x/1.15x/1.24x. In the same run libxml2 DOM reached 28.5 MB/s at 1 MB (~8.6x, derived from page data). A later turbo-on C++-only run (24.09.2026) gives 283.0 vs 271.1 MB/s (1 MB) and 296.5 vs 278.5 (10 MB) against pugixml (~1.04x/~1.06x, derived from page data). Against libxml2 DOM that run gives 37.8 and 38.0 MB/s (~7.5x/~7.8x, derived from page data). The README notes that at 10 MB libsimdxml uses ~8% more CPU than pugixml. The README also states 1.26x/1.35x/1.47x over Rust quick-xml 0.36 at 1/5/10 MB.
corrections.workload: Single-threaded parse of the project's own deterministic synthetic XML (16,824 elements at 1 MB, depth up to 22, attributes, entities, CDATA, comments, PIs) into libsimdxml's structural index. Measured in MB/s and peak RSS against pugixml 1.16 (in-situ DOM), libxml2 DOM, expat SAX and parsers in other languages. Speed numbers are published only for 1/5/10 MB (the 24.09 run covers only 1 and 10 MB). The 15-30 MB corpora are listed but have no published numbers.
corrections.is_fork_of: https://github.com/simdxml/simdxml (C++23 port; README and NOTICE say it is derived from this Rust crate by Christopher Grainger, MIT OR Apache-2.0; not a GitHub fork)
corrections.caveats: The benchmark harness, runners and data generator are not in the public repo, so the numbers cannot be reproduced. No compiler name/version or flags are stated, so this is capped at C. libsimdxml is a lenient, non-validating structural indexer, and nesting deeper than 32 levels gets degraded parent links. libxml2 checks well-formedness and builds a full DOM, so the ~7.5-8.6x libxml2 ratio is not like-for-like; pugixml is the fairer comparison. The README gives the pugixml lead as 1.15-1.24x at base clock, but the later turbo-on run shows only ~4-6% wall-time lead and ~8% more CPU at 10 MB. It is a C++ port of the Rust simdxml crate. 0 stars, repo created 2026-09-07, with no third-party review.

notes: The pugixml figures match the README exactly. I downgraded because the record's 'roughly 8-10x faster than libxml2' is overstated: the page supports ~7.5-8.6x, and nothing reaches 10x. The tier stays C. I also noted that the benchmark code is absent from the repo and that the project is a port of the Rust simdxml crate.

tier_reason: The first-party Google Benchmark code is public (benchmarks/bench_parse.cpp and its mirror benchmarks/bench_yamlcpp.cpp, both using the same inputs from bench_data.h), and GCC 9.4 is stated. Optimization flags are not stated, and the CPU is only 'Intel Xeon' with no model, so it is not A. There is no paper or third-party suite, so it is C.

corrections.compiler_and_flags: GCC 9.4, C++17, Google Benchmark (README). Optimization flags are not stated. CMakeLists.txt sets no default CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE, and the README build is plain 'cmake ..'. yaml-cpp 0.8 is linked from a prebuilt YAML_CPP_DIR whose build type is also unstated.
corrections.caveats: The repo description says the code was written by AI ('本项目代码由AI编写'), and commits are co-authored by an AI tool. The benchmark table was added in commit f1904fc (2026-07-07) and never re-run. Later commits fixed major correctness bugs: flow-parsing infinite loops (07-12), and on 09-08 comments that crashed or truncated parsing, sibling keys swallowed into nested maps, and missing block-scalar support. One known flow-map defect remains. Inputs are tiny (4.5-15 µs parses of a ~75-line config). The 34x/54x 'cached' conversions measure PipeYAML caching repeated as<T>() calls on the same node, which yaml-cpp does not do; they are not parse speedups, and 54x with unstated flags is above the >50x cap. The CPU is the generic 'Intel Xeon' with no model. 0 stars, created 2026-07-03, with no external review or adoption yet.

notes: Every claimed_speedup figure matches the README table exactly, and the benchmark code is symmetric for PipeYAML and yaml-cpp. The tier stays C. I added caveats: the numbers predate substantial correctness fixes, and the build flags for both sides are unknown.
